text.p: Louisiana Land and Exploration Co expects to spud a series of delineation wells to assess an Algerian find that is part of the independent oil and natural gas company's aggressive exploration program, said John Williams, senior vice president of exploration and production.

The company completed an initial well on Block 405 that tested at 15,850 barrels of oil per day (bpd) and 61 million cubic feet of natural gas per day (mmcfd) over in 85-foot of net pay, and is in the process of completing a second well offset to the north, Williams said in an interview.

Depending on the success of that well, known as the MLN-2 well, the company expects to spud at least two additional delineation wells late this year and into 1997 to determine the size of the discovery. "It's obviously one of the biggest pieces of business we've got in the company and we're real excited about that one well we've drilled so far," he said.

"That could be a big field. It could be in the two to three hundred million barrel range, given what we've got mapped right now. And if the well-control confirms what we are mapping, then obviously it's a very significant thing for us with a 65 percent interest in the activity there."

In addition to the delineation wells, LL&E plans to shoot another 600 kilometers of two-dimensional seismic surveys on Block 405, which would satisfy its requirements to shoot seismic on its Algerian blocks, he said.

In addition to the oilfield under the MLN-1 and MLN-2 wells, a map of the Block 405 exploration activity area shows the extension of an Anadarko field to the northeast under LL&E's MLNE-1 well. The company also has found five prospects in the acreage and another encroaching into the field.

LL&E confirmed the extension of the Anadarko discovery with its MLNE-1 well in the northeast corner of Block 405, a section of the northern Sahara covered with huge sand dunes. The well encountered a 50 meter column of oil but tested at only 750 barrels of oil per day and associated gas.

The well also encountered clear water at a depth indicated by wells drilled earlier nearby, he said. "The sand in which the oil/water contact was encountered was not perforated and tested for fear of producing water, although the sand quality was significantly better," Williams said.

The New Orleans-based company expects to drill one or two more wells in this northeast section of the acreage after processing additional seismic tests. "While the test itself was disappointing, the fact that the oilfield apparently extends onto Block 405 was most encouraging," he said.
